source.title: EVA: Towards a universal model of the immune system
source.authors: Scienta Team; Ethan Bandasack; Vincent Bouget; Apolline Bruley; Yannis Cattan; Charlotte Claye; Matthew Corney; Julien Duquesne; Karim El Kanbi; Aziz Fouché; Pierre Marschall; Francesco Strozzi

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure/table text is flattened, but the relevant scaling results are described in the text and tables.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling behavior in a new setting: a biological transcriptomics model trained on gene-expression data, rather than a language model trained on text. It also measures whether downstream task scores change with model size and training.
record.gate_note: The paper reports an EVA-RNA validation-loss scaling fit and downstream performance by model size, so these are included. Other benchmark results unrelated to scaling or downstream scaling predictability are omitted. The text does not test the compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, fixed-parameter architecture variation, or prediction of much larger runs from a fit to small runs.
record.test_reason: The study fits a power law to validation loss against compute for five EVA-RNA gene-expression models (7M–300M), a new modality, which bears on V5. It reports downstream scores at three model sizes (Table 1, Table 11) and over training steps (Fig. 4b), which bears on V6. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors claim clear, predictable scaling of validation loss up to 300M with no plateau. They say pretraining gains carry over to downstream tasks 'in almost all cases' and that profiles vary by task. Their own Table 1/11 show non-monotonic or flat size effects on several tasks, which the conclusion's 'consistently' overstates.
record.recipe_differences: This is gene-expression foundation-model pretraining with masked gene-expression prediction and a zero-inflated negative-binomial objective, not autoregressive text-model pretraining with held-out cross-entropy. The reported fit is validation loss versus compute; no compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is tested.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that scaling profiles vary by downstream task. In the model-size sweep, the endotype score is lower at 300M than at 60M, and zero-shot target efficacy is lower at 60M than at 7M.
record.code_released: An open version of EVA-RNA is released to HuggingFace; URL not stated.
record.problems: The scaling-loss fit is reported without an uncertainty estimate or a separately held-out larger-run prediction. The compute scaling uses five sizes, but batch size and learning rate were adapted across sizes. Several downstream scaling values are shown only in Figure 4b, without exact values in the text. The paper reports that task scaling profiles vary.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant scaling or downstream-scaling results were omitted. Other benchmark comparisons, multimodal ablations, and interpretability results do not measure a claim version here.

untested.parts: Image/video, repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes; scaling in tokens or data (only model size/compute varied).
Explicit functional fit of downstream score vs scale or loss; downstream at 15M and 25M sizes.
No held-out extrapolation to larger runs.
No variation of fitting or setup choices.

missing.what: Per-subtask results by size, many non-monotonic or falling at 300M. Examples: ADA→IFX 0.65/0.56/0.50; endotype RA blood 0.66/0.65/0.52; several molecular-to-clinical subtasks lower at 300M than 60M.
Appendix text claims treatment outcome 0.736 and 'consistent improvement from 7M to 300M'. Table 1 gives 0.650, and the size trend is non-monotonic.
Per-size validation loss and compute values are not given numerically, and 15M/25M models are not evaluated downstream.

record.verdict_notes: The downstream size sweep has only three points and no fit, so 'predictable' is not directly tested. Fig. 4b tracks training steps, and the text likely means the 300M model; these rows bear on V6 only through pretraining loss. The power-law fit has a very small exponent and confounded hyperparameters. Table 11 columns are partly misaligned in the extracted text; values cited from it should be checked.

versions.untested_parts: The study is about gene-expression pretraining, not language models, and does not test held-out language-model cross-entropy as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
It fits a loss-versus-compute curve across five EVA-RNA sizes, but does not report a fit on small runs used to predict separately held-out runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is reported.
Model sizes vary in layers and hidden dimensions, but the study does not compare architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
The study tests transcriptomics/gene-expression pretraining only; it does not test image or video models, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer-learning loss scaling.
Downstream scaling is evaluated on the reported EVA-RNA benchmark tasks and training trajectory, not across other model families or domains.
The study does not systematically vary fitting method, parameter counting, schedule, data, or other setup choices to test sensitivity of exponents or compute-optimal allocation.

rows.subject: EVA-RNA (five-model scaling sweep)
rows.operation_detail: Fit validation loss as a power law of compute across model sizes trained on identical data with consistent hyperparameters; batch size and learning rate were adapted for training stability.

conditions.value: identical pretraining data across model sizes

rows.measure: Validation loss as a function of compute
rows.value: L = 2.515 × C^-0.032; each order-of-magnitude increase in compute reduces validation loss by approximately 7%; no evidence of a plateau at 300M parameters
rows.note: The reported loss is EVA-RNA validation loss for gene-expression pretraining, not language-model held-out cross-entropy.
rows.check: The state is fine. However, the fit has no uncertainty, the exponent is tiny (b=0.032), and it spans only ~1.6 orders of magnitude in parameters. Batch size and learning rate differ across sizes, and per-size loss values are not given.

relationships.reason: Validation loss fits L=2.515·C^-0.032 with no plateau at 300M (r1). The range is narrow and no uncertainty is given.
relationships.display_finding: Validation loss fits L = 2.515·C^-0.032 without a plateau through 300M parameters, over a narrow range without reported uncertainty.

relationships.condition: Gene function, clinical treatment outcome, and molecular perturbation (aggregate) across 7M/60M/300M
relationships.display_finding: Scores increased with size for gene function at 0.387→0.441→0.494, treatment outcome at 0.572→0.613→0.650 and molecular perturbation at 0.511→0.544→0.547.

relationships.condition: Zero-shot target efficacy, endotype stratification, and molecular-to-clinical activity across sizes; per-task training trajectories
relationships.reason: Zero-shot efficacy dips at 60M (0.655→0.619) and endotype drops at 300M (0.799→0.786). Molecular-to-clinical gains mostly 7M→60M. Trajectories plateau for some tasks (r2–r4, r14–r19, r23–r28).
relationships.display_finding: Target efficacy fell from 0.655 to 0.619 at 60M and endotype performance from 0.799 to 0.786 at 300M, while molecular-to-clinical gains concentrated between 7M and 60M and some trajectories plateaued.

relationships.reason: Aggregate Pearson is flat at 0.443/0.444/0.445, so no scale effect is visible (r11–r13).
relationships.display_finding: Aggregate Pearson correlation was nearly unchanged at 0.443, 0.444 and 0.445 for 7M, 60M and 300M models, respectively.

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
